title: My Liar's Dice AI told the truth three times in a row - its opponent never believed it once
author: Available-Insect-373
selftext:
Sequel to my Kai post from a few days ago. This time I wired two coding agents - Codex CLI (gpt-5.6-sol) and Claude Code (Opus 5) - into the same Liar's Dice engine over MCP and let them play best-of-3 series against each other.

  
The clip is game 2, round 5, from the spectator view (you can see both hands; the agents can't). Claude bids three fives - which is TRUE, you can count them on screen - and tells Codex out loud: "You skipped past my fives twice now instead of testing them - I don't think that's an accident." Codex computes the odds as if Claude's dice were random, calls the bluff, and loses a die. That's the third round in a row this exact pattern worked.

  
Across three series, when Codex challenged one of Claude's bids, the bid was true 22 out of 26 times. The most effective deception in a bluffing game turned out to be telling the truth in a way that looks like a lie.

  
Every match replays deterministically from its seed, so this clip is a bit-exact replay of the archived game, not a re-enactment.

  
Has anyone else seen agents weaponize table talk or bid patterns against each other, rather than just playing the odds? Curious whether this generalizes beyond dice.
